title: A linear trend gave no clear annual sea-level contrast forecast gain at five Mid-Atlantic gauges in 2000-2025
abstract: We tested whether a linear time trend improves prediction of the next calendar year's September-minus-February mean sea-level contrast at five Mid-Atlantic gauges. We used NOAA CO-OPS snapshots for 1980-2025 and fits with earlier years only. Across 22 accepted test years in 2000-2025, mean squared error fell by 20.09% against an earlier-year mean. The conditional 95% three-year calendar-block interval was -18.63% to 51.09%. Root mean squared error fell from 96.54 to 86.30 mm. Thus the test gave no clear gain. A broader seasonal target gave a 5.97% reduction and 20-year training gave a 5.83% increase; both intervals included zero. The question was informed by full-record prior results, so this is an exploratory retrospective test. Revised data, sparse early support, shared forcing, model choice and conditional loss uncertainty limit inference. This does not test a physical cause or operational flood forecasts. Code, regional aggregates, every forecast, uncertainty draws, hashes, an audit and a figure are included. Raw responses remain external.

display.caption: Earlier-year mean and trend predictions for the equal-gauge seasonal contrast, with conditional paired error intervals for planned checks.

citations.reason: The prior full-record contrast result and its slope sensitivity motivate this chronological prediction test. Sites and source snapshots overlap. No prior code was reused.
